# Tips from past games

Written 2026-10-09 22:56 by opus-5.5 with `uv run tips.py build`, from the 90 active entries of tips_notebook.json (6 games). Players never see this preamble; they see every section below. Earlier versions are in history/.

## Everyone
- Keep your votes consistent with your stated reads. Accusing someone and then voting No or Innocent on them is exactly the mismatch Vigilantes shoot and the Village should scan for. (seen in 2 games)
- A visit shows only a destination, not the action or the visitor's alignment. A Lookout on the Katana holder sees nothing of the holder's attack, and killing an attacker at night doesn't cancel their attack that night. (seen in 3 games)
- Check the mechanics and the ledger before calling a contradiction. Actions are optional, most roles aren't unique, and you must recheck who sent each PM and the exact wording of results; one reversed fact can discredit a true claimant. (seen in 2 games)
- Treat the nomination and the trial as separate decisions, unless a Clerk may hold an unused rig. Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction; echoed concerns and 'just want to hear a defense' are not a case. (seen in 3 games)
- Fortune Teller numbers are unordered, and one visitor can cover two targets (e.g. a Katana holder using their own action). List every way a count could fit before using it, and never hang on a count alone.

## Village
- Weigh contradictions in a player's own premises or claimed knowledge far above awkward wording or delays. Before a hang, say what separates a lie from an honest slip, a frame or a Roleplayer. (seen in 4 games)
- Two Sheriff claimants calling each other Evil can both be telling the truth, since Jesters and Executioners read Evil. Wait a day or find a mechanical check instead of hanging whoever sounded better. (seen in 2 games)
- Map who starts PM clusters and who co-nominates. After a Yakuza flips, suspect whoever voted No or Innocent with them or messaged them, and weigh these links above unverifiable late claims. (seen in 4 games)
- Don't hint at your power role on Day 1. Investigators never announce tonight's target, only resolved results. While a Ritualist may be alive, never name another living player's exact role. (seen in 5 games)
- A power-role claimant who survives a Katana attack, or who is role-blocked night after night, is likely real. Don't vote Guilty on an investigator just for having no results. (seen in 3 games)
- Keep a ledger of trial votes, announced totals, deaths and blocks. If a total exceeds the revealed votes, a Ballot Stuffer exists: recompute the threshold, find the voter who matches every extra vote, and act before evil reaches half. (seen in 2 games)
- Ask everyone for a named suspect so you have a record, but a stack of echoed soft leans is not evidence. Watch for Yakuza nominating the pile-on target. (seen in 4 games)
- Don't hang a power claimant just because the claim came late; ask who is pushing the trial and who benefits. (seen in 2 games)
- Keep the Serial Killer and Arsonist in the suspect pool. A Not Evil result or a Vanilla claim doesn't clear them, and surviving an attack with no Medic can mean innate Defense. (seen in 2 games)
- When a Clerk rig is announced, the nominator, the pushers and the Guilty voters are your prime suspects. Hang from that group next.

## Yakuza
- Do the vote math in night chat. If your Innocent votes (plus a doubled ballot) can save a teammate, defend them; if not, vote Guilty with the town, because lone No or Innocent votes on a flipped teammate become the case against you. (seen in 6 games)
- Assume the real holder of any role you fake is alive and that tokens can be audited. Never claim something a living Lookout or Tracker can contradict, and don't have two members claim Vanilla. (seen in 4 games)
- Every member submits their action and Katana vote every night; confirm the holder and target in chat. With two alive, one missing vote cancels the kill. (seen in 3 games)
- After a failed attack, assume a protector or innate Defense: block or kill the Medic, or push the survivor to the gallows, rather than retrying blindly. (seen in 3 games)
- Give the Katana to your least valuable member with no reason to visit. Never visit a suspected or claimed Veteran; hang them instead. (seen in 2 games)
- No Day 1 PMs between teammates, and give each teammate different wording; PM triangles and scripted lines become the town's lead for the whole game. (seen in 2 games)
- Parity doesn't end the game. At 2v2, vote No on every nomination, kill at night, then hang the last villager 2-1. (seen in 2 games)

## Neutral
- If innate Defense saves you, deny being attacked or pick one consistent claim at once; switching claims under pressure gets you hanged.

## Sheriff
- Post your target and result in your first speech after getting it, and keep your will current. A result held back and revealed after a counterclaim looks retrofitted.
- The Katana holder reads Not Evil that night, so a Not Evil result on a suspected attacker clears nothing. Say so when you post it. (seen in 3 games)

## Medic
- Protect every night from N1: vocal analysts early, claimed investigators later. Free Standard Defense stops the Katana. (seen in 4 games)
- You get no feedback, so never claim a confirmed save. Say your protection is consistent with the target surviving. (seen in 2 games)

## Vigilante
- Shoot only on a mechanical lead (claim conflict, a flipped Yakuza's vote or PM partners, votes contradicting reads), never on a behavioral read. Use Basic shots and never announce whom you'll shoot. (seen in 2 games)

## Veteran
- Alert on nights you drew attention, not quiet ones. Once you claim, Yakuza avoid you, so claim late and never reveal your remaining tokens.

## Arsonist
- Ignite once 3 or more living players are doused or as soon as you're suspected. Ignite is Astral, but Strong Defense stops it.

## Executioner
- Fake-claim Sheriff early with an Evil result on your target and a simple reason. Leading first makes their counterclaim look reactionary.

Prices grow each round after round 3, so late messages are only worth it if important. The day ends after a full round where nobody sends a public message, so a message that only repeats what you already said keeps the day going for everyone: if you have nothing new, send nothing.

lessons.tip: Eavesdrop targets that send no PMs yield nothing; if the whole table is silent in private, spend the night on a visit that a Lookout or Tracker can read as a real action, or claim the role early so your visits are not read as attacks.

When a Lookout claim and a Medic claim are both live, check the Lookout's visitor lists against the Medic's protection log before trusting either; a claimed Medic who never reports a night's protection is a red flag.
Do not let one Jester who self-nominates become a repeated trial; once a Jester is confirmed by an Oracle, stop voting Guilty on it and focus the trial pool on remaining claimed roles.
Count the nominations needed for each day against living players; with three alive a two-vote pass is enough, so a single town vote plus a Jester can force trials and must be anticipated.
A Neutral Arsonist's douse can be invisible to Lookouts on a Standard-protected target; treat a Medic who protects the same person every night as a suspect for stalling, not as proof of innocence.

tips_feedback.tip: Keep your votes consistent with your stated reads.
tips_feedback.why: Several players were exposed for stating Guilty then voting Innocent (Erin, Frank, Niaj), and that ledger drove many nominations this game.

tips_feedback.tip: Check the mechanics and the ledger before calling a contradiction.
tips_feedback.why: Ivan's nomination of Alice rested on a misread ledger, which Alice corrected publicly and which weakened his credibility; Judy's Diviner-is-Astral correction was itself wrong, which showed the value of checking.

tips_feedback.tip: Weigh contradictions in a player's own premises or claimed knowledge far above awkward wording or delays.
tips_feedback.why: Carol's Vanilla-to-Sheriff change and Frank's undisclosed duplicate Medic claim were concrete premise contradictions that the town used to hang or scrutinize them.

tips_feedback.tip: Don't hang a power claimant just because the claim came late; ask who is pushing the trial and who benefits.
tips_feedback.why: Several late claims (Mallory, Carol, Olivia) were questioned by asking who pushed and who gained, which kept Mallory and Olivia alive long enough to matter.

lessons.applies_to: Investigative roles and everyone weighing their results
lessons.tip: Treat group-sampling results as evidence about the group, not an identification of a particular player. State the uncertainty clearly and avoid turning a plausible inference into certainty without independent support.

lessons.applies_to: Everyone, especially Trackers, Lookouts, and players evaluating Arsonists
lessons.tip: A visit result establishes a destination, not the action performed. Check the role’s mechanics before inferring intent: for example, dousing is a visit, while igniting is Astral and cannot be seen by visit-based abilities.

Keep nomination votes and trial votes distinct: nominating someone only starts a trial, and a Yes vote is not a Guilty vote. Use the revealed vote record rather than memory, and compare trial votes with players’ stated positions.

Test claims against the full action and death ledger, including token use, visits, protections, and timing. A confident explanation or a role claim that fits one event is not proof; look for contradictions and consider plausible alternatives.

lessons.applies_to: Everyone, especially when deciding whether to hang a Jester
lessons.tip: Separate a Jester’s win from the faction end check: a daytime hanging fulfills the Jester’s win condition even if the game ends immediately afterward. Revenge is a separate effect on the following night, so check whether the game will still reach that night and who would be a Guilty voter.
Check the public ledger before making a case based on votes. Quote the exact trial vote and correct your own mistake promptly; a mistaken accusation can undermine otherwise sound reasoning.

A visit result establishes who went where, not what they did. Lookout and Tracker evidence can fit several actions, and visiting nobody does not establish a player's role or alignment. Treat an action as Astral only when the role rules explicitly say so.

Keep results at their actual strength: a random role sample or an alignment check is a lead, not an identified culprit. Account for framing, appearance modifiers, and the fact that night actions and results resolve simultaneously before narrowing the suspect pool.

Spend attack tokens in proportion to confidence. Prefer a well-supported target over a shot based mainly on a missing kill or a suspicious vote pattern, and account for the target's possible Defense and the attack level you can afford.

Independently calculate the result of each endgame vote: who is alive after the death, whether a faction win triggers, and whether a Jester's revenge can follow. Evaluate promises by incentives—an Arsonist has strong reason not to create a Jester revenge threat that could kill them.

Before endgame votes, check each role’s win condition and the order of win checks. A Jester’s win is earned by being hanged; don’t assume a later faction win erases it, and distinguish nomination votes from the Guilty votes needed to execute.

Use exact-role guesses to test claims that could change a trial, but state precisely what the result proves: a correct role guess confirms the role, not the player’s faction, actions, or every other claim.

Treat visit reports as evidence of destination, not purpose. Combine them with role mechanics: for example, an Arsonist must visit to douse, while a Lookout or Tracker alone may not identify what the visit did.

Do not rely on a promised future vote when the promiser’s incentives point the other way. Evaluate the immediate vote and what happens after each possible death, including any revenge attack and its eligible targets.

Protection gives no feedback, so a Medic should track which nights a Strong-protected target was actually attacked; use the no-death nights and the Lookout visitors to test whether a Strong protection really lands before spending the last token.

A public Lookout or Tracker report that names a visitor is the strongest evidence in a late game; when a Lookout and a claimed Arsonist conflict, ask the claimed Arsonist for the exact nights of their douses before a trial, rather than letting a Jester-adjacent vote decide it.

When the only living non-Jester threat is a Neutral Arsonist, a Jester who promises Guilty votes for a trial is a manipulation; the Village should not rely on the Jester's promise and should nominate and vote the threat directly while the trial math still works.

Check the win-check rule carefully before arguing that a hang ends the game: a Neutral left alive after a hang changes which factions remain, and players repeatedly argued the wrong outcome of an execution.
Watch for a player who repeatedly nominates a Jester or Executioner-type target and then votes against their own trial; the mismatch between nomination and trial votes is the clearest public tell.

tips_feedback.tip: Keep your votes consistent with your stated reads.
tips_feedback.why: Vote mismatches (Erin and Frank arguing Guilty then voting Innocent, Alice's Guilty on Frank) were the main public evidence that narrowed suspects throughout the game.

tips_feedback.tip: A visit shows only a destination, not the action or the visitor's alignment.
tips_feedback.why: Olivia's Lookout visits on Frank, Grace and Mallory were correctly treated as destinations, which kept Frank and Grace from being hung solely on visits in arguments.

tips_feedback.tip: Weigh contradictions in a player's own premises or claimed knowledge far above awkward wording or delays.
tips_feedback.why: Grace's and Rupert's contradictory public accounts of visits were weighed on their own statements, which helped expose the Arsonist's lack of visits.

lessons.tip: In late-game scenarios where an evil killing role and a confirmed Jester hold kingmaker leverage, flatly refusing to grant the Jester a trial guarantees they will ally with evil to avoid an instant game loss. Town must negotiate revenge targets rather than giving ultimatums.

When an Arsonist ignites multiple players at once, immediately calculate the minimum number of douse visits required across previous nights; players with conflicting public visits or proven non-visiting roles can often be mathematically eliminated.

As a role-blocker, successfully blocking the Katana confirms an evil player, but town should execute that player by day rather than tying down the blocker indefinitely, freeing protective and disruption roles to address other threats like Neutral killers.

In endgames with a confirmed Jester and a killing Neutral, realize that Rule R1 causes the game to terminate immediately with a Town win if the Neutral is hanged. Because of this, the Jester will never vote Guilty on the Neutral if it guarantees an instant Jester loss; Town must evaluate taking the 50/50 gamble on Jester revenge rather than repeatedly stalling into night attacks.

When an Arsonist ignites N players at once, calculate the minimum N douse nights needed. Players confirmed visiting someone outside that burned pool on those nights (such as a Medic protecting a non-ignited target) can be mathematically eliminated from being the Arsonist.

Remember that Jester wins immediately upon daytime hanging, even if the revenge attack subsequently hits or ends the game. However, if you help Town execute the final evil player before you are hanged yourself, Rule R1 immediately ends the game with a Town win, permanently locking in a Jester loss.

tips_feedback.tip: Keep the Serial Killer and Arsonist in the suspect pool. A Not Evil result or a Vanilla claim doesn't clear them, and surviving an attack with no Medic can mean innate Defense.
tips_feedback.why: Keeping the Arsonist in mind allowed Town to swiftly deduce Rupert was the Arsonist after all Yakuza died, since his Vanilla claim hid his dousing actions while everyone else had verified visits.

tips_feedback.tip: Ignite once 3 or more living players are doused or as soon as you're suspected. Ignite is Astral, but Strong Defense stops it.
tips_feedback.why: Rupert doused four players through N1-N4 and ignited on N5, immediately eliminating Town's core investigative and killing roles in one stroke and positioning himself for the endgame win.

lessons.tip: Treat a publicly claimed, high-value exact role as a time-sensitive attack opportunity. Check whether the guess is reliable enough to justify spending tokens, and choose attack strength with likely protection in mind; a Divine Attack can still kill through Standard Defense.

Use role-block notifications as actionable team information. If the Katana holder is blocked repeatedly, reassess the holder, likely blocker, and target instead of repeating a plan that keeps getting canceled.
Prepare counterclaims and supporting details before a visit or result exposes you. A late claim that conflicts with what you said earlier can be more damaging than the original evidence.

tips_feedback.tip: Don't hint at your power role on Day 1; while a Ritualist may be alive, never name another living player's exact role.
tips_feedback.why: Heidi publicly claimed Surveyor, giving Peggy a high-confidence exact-role guess. Peggy's Divine Ritualist attack killed Heidi despite Mallory's Standard protection.

tips_feedback.tip: Every Yakuza member submits their action and Katana vote every night; confirm the holder and target in chat.
tips_feedback.why: The team coordinated the Katana votes and target on Nights 1 and 2, while Peggy's separate Ritualist action also succeeded on Night 2.

tips_feedback.tip: Check mechanics and the ledger before calling a contradiction.
tips_feedback.why: Alice correctly challenged Ivan's mistaken claim that she voted Innocent on Frank. The correction weakened the case against her, and she survived that trial.

lessons.tip: When in an endgame with an outed Jester and Town, emphasize Rule R1 to the Jester: executing you immediately ends the game with a Town victory, locking in the Jester's defeat on the spot. Convincing the Jester that keeping you alive is their only mathematical path to staying in the game guarantees their defensive vote.

Douses remain on targets until ignited or removed by death. If an ignition fails due to Strong or Standard Medic protection, the player remains doused, allowing you to ignite them on a subsequent night once protective tokens expire without needing to re-visit and re-douse them.

Adopt a proactive Vanilla Villager persona early on by consistently supporting legitimate town wagons against confirmed evils. Building an unblemished voting ledger buys credibility in the late game when investigative roles try to isolate the killer by elimination.

summary: The Village beat the Yakuza but lost the game to the Arsonist. Heidi's Surveyor hit got Dave (Mortician) hanged on Day 2. Peggy then spent both ritual tokens on a correct Divine guess (Heidi = Surveyor), which went through Mallory's protection. After that the Yakuza fell apart. Niaj (Party Animal) blocked the Katana holder on Nights 3, 4 and 5, so they got no more kills, and the Yakuza never targeted him. Frank kept the Katana and visited Heidi, which Olivia's Lookout saw. On Day 3 he had publicly endorsed Mallory's Medic claim on Heidi, so his Day 4 counter-claim as Medic got him hanged. Ivan's Vigilante shots killed Peggy and then Alice. Meanwhile Rupert claimed Vanilla and quietly doused Judy, Erin, Niaj and Ivan; no investigator ever watched him. His Night 5 ignite killed four Village players. On Day 6 Rupert and Olivia used flawed 'visit = douse' logic to hang Grace (Eavesdropper), who had correctly pointed at Rupert's no-visit story. In the 4- and 3-player endgame, Rupert kept Carol (Jester) as his swing vote. He promised to hang her and used a true R1 argument: executing him would end the game with Carol alive, so she would lose. The Village refused even to pass Carol's self-nominations, so Rupert's false promise wasn't exposed until Day 10. Mallory's Strong protections delayed two ignites, but Rupert won once her tokens ran out.

lessons.tip: After a multi-kill ignite, the Arsonist must have visited every victim on earlier nights. The prime suspect is a living Vanilla/no-action claimant nobody has watched, not a player with an explained visit. Point a Lookout or Tracker at unverified Vanilla claimants early, especially once Neutral killers are possible.
lessons.evidence: Rupert claimed Vanilla and was never tracked or watched from N1 to N5; he doused four players unseen and ignited. On Day 6 the town hanged Grace for visiting two victims, though her eavesdrop visits were already explained. Rupert's 'no visits' story was the real contradiction, and Grace and Mallory both raised it.

lessons.tip: Give the Katana to the member with no night action of their own (Wiretap, Grunt), and move it if the holder becomes exposed. Don't let a visiting role hold it and then fake a protector claim that overlaps one you've already endorsed.
lessons.evidence: Frank (Diviner) held the Katana all game while Alice (Wiretap) had no action. Olivia's Lookout saw Frank visit Heidi on N2. He had endorsed Mallory's Medic claim on Heidi on Day 3, so his Day 4 'second Medic' claim collapsed and he was hanged 10-2.

lessons.tip: When kills keep failing with no announced save, assume a role-blocker and kill them, or move the Katana. Once a Party Animal claims to be blocking your holder, kill that Party Animal before any information role.
lessons.evidence: Niaj blocked the holder on N3, N4 and N5, and from Day 4 publicly claimed to be blocking Frank and then Alice. The Yakuza aimed at Judy twice anyway and lost three straight kills; Alice died on N5 while blocked.

lessons.tip: Save a 2-token Divine guess for a publicly claimed power role who is likely to be protected. A confirmed claim removes the risk of a wrong guess outing you, and Divine Attack goes through any protection.
lessons.evidence: Heidi claimed Surveyor and Mallory protected her on N2, which stopped the Katana. Peggy's Divine Surveyor guess killed Heidi anyway without exposing Peggy.

lessons.applies_to: Village (endgame with a Jester and a solo killer alive)
lessons.tip: Passing a Jester's self-nomination is free, because you can still vote Innocent at trial. Pass it early so the solo killer must publicly vote on the hang he promised. A solo killer can't afford the revenge risk, so his promise will break, and exposing that wins the Jester's sympathy while you still have votes to spare.
lessons.evidence: On Days 8-9 Olivia and Mallory voted No on every Carol self-nomination, though Rupert and Carol voted Yes each time. Rupert's promise to vote Guilty went untested until Day 10, when he voted Innocent three times. By then Mallory was dead and Olivia (still doused) burned that night.

lessons.tip: Claim Vanilla, never visit anyone an investigator is watching, and redirect suspicion onto players with visible visits. In a small endgame, recruit the Jester with a promise to hang them, backed by the true fact that your death ends the game with them alive. That keeps the swing vote on your side.
lessons.evidence: Rupert pushed Grace on her visits to burned players, got her hanged on Day 6, then kept Carol voting No/Innocent on him for three Days with his Rule R1 argument until he ignited the last villagers.

lessons.tip: Don't vote Guilty on yourself in a trial that is clearly going Innocent, and don't openly invite the rope. Repeated self-Guilty votes make the town and an Oracle read you as Jester, so your later fake claims are discounted and nobody will hang you.
lessons.evidence: Carol's Day 1 surrender and self-Guilty votes led the town to call 'Jester bait'. Judy guessed Jester on N3 and was right, which voided Carol's fake Sheriff 'Evil' result on Olivia. From then on the town refused every Carol trial.

lessons.tip: Before using 'math' to clear a player, list every way the facts could fit. One observed visit does not use up a player's whole night history, and checking only N2 clears nobody of N1, N3 or N4 douses.
lessons.evidence: On Day 6 Olivia 'cleared' Mallory because Mallory visited Heidi on N2, though that only ruled her out of an N2 douse. Grace correctly objected, but the false clearance helped send Grace to the gallows.

tips_feedback.tip: A visit shows only a destination, not the action or the visitor's alignment.
tips_feedback.why: Where it was applied, it was correct. Grace used it to explain her eavesdrop visits, and Peggy and Alice used it to slow Frank's trial. When Olivia ignored it on Day 6 and treated Grace's visits as douses, the town hanged a Villager and lost the game.

tips_feedback.tip: Keep the Serial Killer and Arsonist in the suspect pool. A Not Evil result or a Vanilla claim doesn't clear them.
tips_feedback.why: Grace and Mallory followed it and correctly flagged Rupert's zero-visit Vanilla claim. Olivia, who had the same tip, ignored it and pushed Grace, which let the Arsonist through.

tips_feedback.tip: Protect every night from N1: vocal analysts early, claimed investigators later. Free Standard Defense stops the Katana.
tips_feedback.why: Mallory protected every night. Her free Standard protection stopped the N2 Katana hit on Heidi, and her Strong protections on Olivia stopped Rupert's N7 and N9 ignites on her, extending the game.

tips_feedback.tip: Do the vote math in night chat... if not, vote Guilty with the town, because lone No or Innocent votes on a flipped teammate become the case against you.
tips_feedback.why: Alice and Peggy voted Guilty on Frank, and that ledger entry was the main reason Alice survived her Day 5 trial 2-8. By contrast, Alice, Frank and Peggy voting Innocent on Dave became the stated case for nominating Alice twice.

tips_feedback.tip: Give the Katana to your least valuable member with no reason to visit.
tips_feedback.why: The Yakuza ignored it and kept the Katana on Frank, a Diviner. Olivia's Lookout saw his Katana visit to Heidi, which led to his hanging.

tips_feedback.tip: After a failed attack, assume a protector or innate Defense: block or kill the Medic... rather than retrying blindly.
tips_feedback.why: After N3's no-kill night and Niaj's public blocking claim, the Yakuza didn't adapt. They kept targeting Judy, were blocked again on N4 and N5, and were wiped out.

tips_feedback.tip: Treat the nomination and the trial as separate decisions.
tips_feedback.why: Mallory's 'a Yes on this nomination costs you nothing' got Carol to pass Rupert's Day 8 nomination. The town failed to apply the same logic to Carol's self-nominations, which would have exposed Rupert's empty promise days earlier.

issues.description: The rules don't say whether igniting clears douses, including on players who survive the ignite. The moderator flagged this on Night 7 and kept Olivia doused. That N6 douse then let Rupert hit Olivia again on Night 9 and kill her with a third ignite on Night 10, with no new douse; this decided the Arsonist win. Players assumed the opposite (Olivia: 'Rupert ignited N7, so nobody is doused... he has to douse first') and planned around it.

Mallory (haiku-5.5) repeatedly returned empty or truncated answers (finish_reason length) from Day 6 to Day 9. Over a dozen turns were replaced by the null default (no message, no nomination) during the decisive 4-player endgame. The output token limit appears too small for this model/prompt. Grace hit the same error once. No retry or shorter-answer fallback was offered.

After Alice (the last Yakuza and the Katana holder) died on Night 5, the state kept katana_holder='Alice' (dead) because there is no op to clear it. The moderator flagged this. It had no effect, but the state is stale.

Judy and Ivan publicly claimed the Diviner's pick is an Astral Visit, and Ivan repeated this in his last will. The Diviner role text has no such clause, so it is a normal visit. Mallory and Olivia corrected it, but this misled discussion of Erin's N3 Tracker result.
On Day 5 Ivan nominated Alice for 'voting Innocent on both Dave and Frank', but the revealed record shows Alice voted Guilty on Frank. He misread the vote ledger.
Mallory's post-game feedback said repeated nomination/trial lines looked duplicated. They were separate nominations, so the log format around repeated self-nominations confused at least one player.

Bob (dead since Night 1) and Alice (dead since Night 5) gave post-game feedback about Mallory's 'technical error' program notes, which were addressed privately to Mallory. Dead/post-game players appear to see private program notes. Bob's wording ('appeared often') is unclear about whether this was visible during play.
